title: Rorty
keyWorks: Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature (1979)
summary: Richard Rorty was an American philosopher who carried on the pragmatist tradition of James and Dewey. He held that language is not a mirror of reality but a set of tools, and that we have no final, eternal answers. Instead he proposed living with "irony" towards our own convictions, creating ourselves through new descriptions, and building solidarity by trying to reduce cruelty and humiliation.
onEmotions: Rorty didn't develop a separate theory of emotions, but his ideas change a lot about how we can look at feelings. He believed we describe ourselves with a "final vocabulary" — words like "good", "real", "loser", beyond which our explanations usually don't go. The "ironist" understands that her vocabulary is only one of many and that one can "redescribe" oneself. So no painful description of yourself is the final truth. At the same time, Rorty stressed that pain and humiliation are what all human beings share, and that solidarity is born of attention to the particular details of other people's suffering.

anxiety.text: William James called true whatever "pays" in practice, and his heir Rorty added: the world issues no certificates about the future to anyone. When what lies ahead is unclear, wanting a firm guarantee is deeply human. But there is no "view from nowhere" from which to check once and for all what will happen. The pragmatists proposed another way of seeing beliefs: not as mirror copies of reality but as tools for action. Anxiety often demands the impossible — final certainty before a step is taken. Rorty suggested changing the question: not "is it true that everything will end badly?" but "which description of the situation will help me take the next step?" The anxiety doesn't vanish, but it stops being a verdict and becomes one of the voices in a conversation.
anxiety.practice: Say the anxious thought out loud, then two more descriptions of the same situation, as you'd tell them to a friend over tea. Which of the three suggests one small step?

fear.text: Rorty looked for what unites all human beings and found neither reason nor soul but vulnerability: anyone can be wounded by pain and humiliation. Your fear is the voice of exactly this vulnerability, the voice of a creature that can be hurt. For Rorty there is no shared "human essence" to lean on, but there is a shared fragility. Solidarity is built on it — on the ability to see others as "fellow sufferers". So fear doesn't cut you off from people; it connects you to them: many others are afraid of something similar right now. Fear shows what is vulnerable and precious to you. You don't have to hide it; you can acknowledge it and let it remind you that you are not the only one who gets scared.
fear.practice: Picture one person who is probably afraid of something similar right now. Silently tell them one encouraging sentence — then repeat it to yourself.

sadness.text: Rorty read Freud almost as a poet: Freud, he said, let us see any life as a poem rather than as a particular case of a general formula. Every life is idiosyncratic — made of its own connections, memories and words, unlike any other. So your sadness needs no justification, and it doesn't have to be filed under a general label like "something is wrong with me". It can be looked at in detail: what exactly is it about, which images and places belong to it? Rorty generally trusted the concrete more than the general — the novel more than the treatise. When sadness gets its own precise words, it becomes part of your story rather than an impersonal verdict. It can be lived through as a chapter that has its own meaning, even if that meaning is not yet clear.
sadness.practice: Go to the window and find three details that chime with your sadness: a colour, a sound, a movement. Name them silently — precise words instead of a general label.

grief.text: Rorty offers no consolation of another world, but he does offer an image: the self is a web of beliefs, desires and words that we weave together with other people. Grief is one of the heaviest things a person goes through, and no philosophy should hurry it. Rorty did not say that loss "has a higher meaning". But there is something important in his image: the one you have lost remains woven into your web — in your words, jokes, habits, in the way you look at the world. After all, we speak with words that someone once gave us. This doesn't cancel the pain of absence. But loss doesn't erase what was between you: it goes on speaking through you.
grief.practice: Say out loud one little word or phrase you inherited from this person. Listen to how it sounds in your voice.

loneliness.text: Novels and reportage, Rorty believed, do more for solidarity than philosophical treatises: they show someone else's life in detail, and strangers suddenly become our own. In loneliness it is easy to believe that you are cut off from others by your very nature, and that hurts. But for Rorty the sense of "we" is not hidden in some shared human essence waiting to be found. It is made: through imagination, through interest in the concrete details of other people's lives, their pain and joy. Loneliness, then, is not a verdict on you but a state in which the bridges haven't been built yet. They are built gradually, in small steps of attention — towards others and from others. And what you feel now, very many people are feeling right now: that is already the beginning of a "we".
loneliness.practice: Open any book or article about someone quite unlike you and read one page. Find one detail in which you recognise them.

quote.text: Solidarity is not discovered by reflection but created. It is created by increasing our sensitivity to the particular details of the pain and humiliation of other, unfamiliar sorts of people.
quote.author: Richard Rorty

anger.text: "A liberal is someone who thinks cruelty is the worst thing we do" — Rorty took this definition from Judith Shklar and held to it all his life. So he did not consider indignation unworthy: your anger may be a legitimate response to injustice or cruelty. It is worth asking it: what concrete cruelty or humiliation is it pointing to? Rorty distrusted big abstract theories and preferred gradual, concrete improvements. Anger can become fuel for such a step. But Rorty saw the other side too: in anger it is easy to start "redescribing" the other person in humiliating words, and so to become a source of cruelty yourself. You can acknowledge your anger fully — and choose to let it serve the reduction of pain rather than its multiplication.
anger.practice: Say silently one sentence about what caused the hurt — without labels for the other person. Then name one small step towards putting it right.

quote.text: Liberals are the people who think that cruelty is the worst thing we do.
quote.author: Richard Rorty (following Judith Shklar)

shame.text: Rorty noticed that a person can be deeply wounded without being touched: it is enough to "redescribe" them, making what mattered to them look ridiculous or worthless. Shame is a very painful feeling and deserves gentleness. Often it is the moment when other people's words about us become our inner verdict. But Rorty has an answer too. He believed that no language of description — neither ours nor anyone else's — is the final truth about a person. Any description can be revised. This doesn't mean nothing matters; it means that the voice shaming you is one description, not the last word. You can ask: whose language is my shame speaking? And try to talk about yourself in your own words.
shame.practice: Write down the sentence your shame speaks in and sign it with whose voice it is. Below, describe the same situation as you would for a close friend.

quote.text: The best way to cause people long-lasting pain is to humiliate them by making the things that seemed most important to them look futile, obsolete, and powerless.
quote.author: Richard Rorty

guilt.text: Justice, for Rorty, is "enlarged loyalty": a faithfulness that begins with those close to us and gradually extends to an ever wider circle of people. Morality, for him, does not descend from an eternal law or a cosmic judge; obligations arise from belonging to particular "we"s — family, friends, communities. The feeling of guilt says that you care, and that in itself matters. If we carry Rorty's thought further, guilt is not a verdict on your essence but a signal of a broken connection with particular people. And a connection, unlike a verdict, can be restored: with a word, an act, attention. Rorty was a pragmatist: he was interested not in "how bad am I" but in "what can be done next".
guilt.practice: Make one small gesture towards the person your guilt concerns: a short message, a call, or at least the first sentence of an apology said silently to yourself.

envy.text: Harold Bloom wrote of the "strong poet", horrified at the thought of being merely a copy of a predecessor — and Rorty turned this into an image of human life in general. Everyone feels envy, and it doesn't make you a bad person. Rorty believed there is no single scale on which lives could be measured and compared: no "final" vocabulary that decides whose life is more correct. Envy, though, often measures us by someone else's yardstick. But it can also hint at something valuable: which word, which possibility you would like to see in your own story. Then it can be turned from a comparison into a question about your own language and your own life.
envy.practice: Imagine being offered the whole life of the person you envy — with their mornings, worries, relatives. Which one detail would you keep for yourself, and what would you turn down?

emptiness.text: Rorty claimed, without any tragic tone, that beneath our beliefs and desires there is no hidden "true self" waiting to be dug up. In emptiness and apathy it is hard even to want anything, and this thought may frighten at first. But it has a gentle side: emptiness is then no verdict on your essence. Rorty described language as a living process: new metaphors are born, then become familiar, "die" and turn into ordinary words. Perhaps emptiness is a time when the old language you used to describe your life has worn out and a new one hasn't appeared yet. Such transitions can be slow. There is no need to hurry them by searching for "the main meaning"; it is enough to notice small glimmers of interest, from which new words grow over time.
emptiness.practice: Step outside for five minutes or walk around the room, looking for nothing. If anything catches your eye even slightly — just note: there's a glimmer.

confusion.text: Ask someone why they live the way they do, and after a couple of "why"s they will hit words like "kind", "genuine", "success". Rorty called such a set a "final vocabulary": explanations usually go no further than these words. An "ironist", for him, is someone who understands that their vocabulary is one of many and therefore doubts it. For the ironist, being at a loss is almost a working condition, if an unpleasant one. It may mean that you have ended up between vocabularies: the old words no longer hold, and new ones haven't formed yet. This is not a failure but a moment of growth. Rorty did not demand a final answer; he suggested continuing the conversation and trying new descriptions until one of them begins to help you live.
confusion.practice: Name silently three to five words that used to explain to you how to live and now seem shaky. Decide nothing — just stay with them for a minute.

quote.text: She has radical and continuing doubts about the final vocabulary she currently uses, because she has been impressed by other vocabularies.
quote.author: Richard Rorty (on the "ironist")

fatigue.text: "Who needs this, and why?" — that is how Dewey, Rorty's favourite philosopher, suggested questioning any "must". Both opposed the idea that everything in life has to be justified before a final tribunal — Truth, Reason, a higher law. Fatigue and burnout are real. But part of the exhaustion comes from the feeling that our "have to"s are set by the very nature of things. The language of endless productivity seems natural, although it is only one of the vocabularies of our age, not a law of the world. Pragmatism doesn't cancel the real workload, but it can remove an extra burden — the feeling that rest must be earned. Rest needs no metaphysical justification, any more than sleep or warm evening light does.
fatigue.practice: Pick one exhausting "I must" and for today rename it "it would be nice to". Then sit for five minutes without earning anything.

boredom.text: Rorty loved Michael Oakeshott's phrase "the conversation of mankind" — a conversation without an ending, in which new voices and unexpected metaphors are what matter most. The philosophy he liked he called "edifying": its task is not to build a final system but to keep the conversation from freezing. Boredom can be agonising: everything is familiar, everything has been said. This seems to be exactly the feeling that the conversation has dried up: all descriptions of the world have become habitual and no longer surprise. It's not your fault but rather a hunger for new language. Rorty believed that novels, poems, other cultures and unlike people can renew our vocabulary. Boredom, then, is not emptiness but an invitation: somewhere nearby are words you haven't heard yet.
boredom.practice: Read one page of something far outside your usual circle — poetry, a science article, a stranger's blog. Take away one word that caught you.

joy.text: As a teenager Rorty roamed the mountains of north-western New Jersey looking for wild orchids — and agonised that this did nothing to help the fight for justice. That is the subject of his essay "Trotsky and the Wild Orchids". He spent a long time trying to join the two loves in one theory and finally decided it wasn't necessary. Private joy — in orchids, music, books — doesn't have to prove its social usefulness. Rorty distinguished the "private" (self-creation, one's own peculiar passions) from the "public" (reducing the suffering of others) and believed that a life needs both. Your joy needs no justification: you can simply accept it and live it — even if it seems strange, small or incomprehensible to others.
joy.practice: Name your "wild orchid" — something that delights you without any use at all — and give it at least a couple of minutes today.

love.text: Moral progress, for Rorty, is driven less by arguments than by "sentimental education" — by stories and closeness that widen the circle of those we care about. Love and tenderness, in this sense, are not irrational but the very material of moral life. Rorty described justice as enlarged loyalty: it all begins with love for particular people nearby and can then grow. Your love is not a private trifle against the background of "serious" things; it is what all serious things are made of. And its details — how a person laughs, what they love, what they fear — are exactly what makes them real to you. Rorty trusted such details more than any principles.
love.practice: Tell someone close to you one concrete detail you love about them — not "you're great", but about their laugh, a pet phrase, a habit.

gratitude.text: The first chapters of Rorty's "Contingency, Irony, and Solidarity" sound almost like an incantation: the contingency of language, the contingency of selfhood, the contingency of community. All of it could have been quite different; nothing we have was guaranteed by the laws of being. Rorty dreamed of a culture that no longer worships anything as a divinity, but gratitude does not disappear because of that. It turns to people and to chance: to those who gave us words, habits, support, and to a lucky run of circumstances. Awareness of contingency doesn't devalue the good; it sharpens it: this might not have happened, and yet it did. There is nothing metaphysical in this warmth — only people and luck.
gratitude.practice: Thank one person today from whom you have kept a word, a thought or a habit: in person, by phone, or silently if they are far away.

hope.text: One of Rorty's collections is called "Philosophy and Social Hope", and the title holds his programme: to replace the centuries-old search for final knowledge with hope. Instead of asking "what is reality really like?", pragmatism asks "what future do we want, and can we build it?" Such hope needs no guarantees. It doesn't rest on the certainty that history is bound to move towards the better, but it doesn't give up in the absence of such certainty either. Rorty called this something like "romance about the future". Your hope, then, is not naivety but a way of keeping the future open. It can be sustained by concrete images and small steps, without demanding promises from it.
hope.practice: Close your eyes and picture one small future you want — in detail: what kind of morning, what light, who is nearby. Stay in that picture for a minute.

nostalgia.text: Nietzsche dreamed of turning every "it was" into "thus I willed it", and Rorty took up the thought: a person creates themselves by redescribing their story — not denying the past but finding their own language for it. Nostalgia, tender and bitter, is a longing not only for a time but also for a vocabulary in which the world once fell into a clear picture. That vocabulary cannot be brought back whole, but it can be reread. The past is not frozen: its meaning changes with each new telling of it. And what was dear can become support for the present, not only a cause for sadness.
nostalgia.practice: Tell someone about one precious moment from the past and end the story with: "…and today it lives in me as…"

craving.text: William James, whose pragmatism Rorty inherited, called habit the "enormous fly-wheel" of life, and beliefs habits of action. A sharp craving, "I want it right now", speaks a very confident language: "this is unbearable without it", "only this will help". Rorty didn't write about craving directly, but he would probably see here one description of the moment, not the final truth about it. The ironist can notice: "right now this vocabulary is speaking in me". Craving is like a wave: it rises, peaks and subsides. If you name it differently and notice its beginning, a little room appears between desire and action. In that room you can already choose.
craving.practice: Put a palm on your chest and tell yourself: "A wave of wanting is rising; it has a beginning and it will have an end." Breathe and watch how it changes over the next few minutes.

addiction.text: The self, for Rorty, is not a kernel hidden in the depths but a web of beliefs, desires and habits woven by contingent circumstances. So addiction is not a moral failure and not proof of a "bad nature": there simply is no hidden "true self" that could turn out to be spoiled. Such a web can't be rewoven in a day, but it can be retied gradually, thread by thread. And we change not alone but inside a "we". Communities of people who know this experience from the inside and talk about it in a shared language — mutual-help groups, for instance — create the solidarity he wrote about. A life organised around one thing can slowly grow new connections and new descriptions of oneself.
addiction.practice: Think of a person or a group where such experience is talked about without judgement. Decide nothing — just note that such places exist and that there is a chair for you in them.

hangover.text: Cruelty is the worst thing we do, Rorty believed; if we carry his thought further, that includes cruelty towards oneself. The morning after can be hard: the body aches, and inside there is anxiety, shame, scraps of memory. And the inner voice often speaks a humiliating language: "I'm worthless", "everything is ruined". The ironist knows that the harshest descriptions are not the final truth: this is one possible vocabulary, and right now it is louder than the rest because you feel bad. You needn't either justify yesterday or punish yourself. You can simply live through this morning, treat yourself gently and later, more calmly, decide what you want to understand from it.
hangover.practice: Catch the harshest sentence you are saying to yourself today and say it again — the way you would to a friend on the same kind of morning.

euphoria.text: Rorty's "strong poet" is someone who finds words that didn't exist before and suddenly sees the world anew. Rorty admired such moments: a new metaphor, in his view, lets us see the familiar differently. A burst of euphoria can resemble this: the world is suddenly redescribed, and there is a lot of air in the new description. There's no need to spoil it with suspicion. But it is worth not only living it but also remembering a little: which words, images, thoughts have come to you now. You don't have to make big decisions on this wave — it is enough to gather the finds. The high will pass, as everything does, but the words found in it may stay and prove useful later.
euphoria.practice: Write down one phrase or image this high suggests, and date it. Keep it — not as a promise, but as a find.

crash.text: Donald Davidson, Rorty's interlocutor, described the life of metaphors: a new one first astonishes, then grows familiar and "dies", becoming an ordinary word. The drop after a high can be sharp and bitter: a moment ago everything shone, and now it's grey. Our experiences have a similar cycle: the vivid inevitably becomes everyday. This doesn't mean the high was a deception and the low is the "real" truth. Neither of these states is the final description of your life. Rorty distrusted the words "actually, everything is…" with which we sum things up. The low is one chapter, not the ending. You can give yourself time and not draw big conclusions at the greyest moment.
crash.practice: Do yourself one small kindness today — a warm shower, a cup of tea, a short walk — and silently name one thing from the high you want to keep.

panic.text: Pain, Rorty wrote, lies before language: it is what unites us with all people and even with animals, who do not speak. In panic this is felt in the body: the heart pounds, breathing falters, it seems something irreparable is about to happen. At such moments there's no room for theories, and the fact that words don't help right now is not your failure. A wave of panic usually builds, peaks and subsides within a few minutes. The pragmatism Rorty held to advises doing what works right now and making sense of it later. Plain names of things bring us back into the shared world: the words we use together with others become support again.
panic.practice: Put your feet flat on the floor and make the out-breath longer than the in-breath. Name out loud five objects around you in the simplest words everyone shares: "table", "window", "cup".

dread.text: Rorty dreamed of a culture in which nothing is written with a capital letter — neither Truth, nor Reason, nor Meaning. When the question "what's the point of it all?" overwhelms you, he would honestly admit: the structure of the universe holds no written answer, no "non-human authority" guaranteeing meaning. But he didn't consider this a catastrophe. Meaning was never hidden in the depths of the world: people have always created it together — in friendship, care, work, conversation, in attempts to make someone else's pain smaller. The absence of a guarantee from above doesn't cancel what is done here, between people. No final answer is needed today. You can let the question be — and lean on something small and close that matters to you simply because you care.
dread.practice: Think of one person or one pursuit that matters to you not because the universe says so but simply because it is dear. Send that person a short hello, or touch that pursuit for a minute.

fomo.text: The feed shows other people's lives in their best description, while you see your own from the inside, with all its weekday details — Rorty, who knew the power of redescription, would spot this imbalance at once. He believed there is no single "right" or "best" life: there are many vocabularies, and none is final. Private self-creation, for Rorty, is idiosyncratic: everyone has their own path and their own "wild orchids". The feeling that everyone else lives more interestingly imposes someone else's vocabulary — "full", "successful", "where it's happening" — as the only possible one. You can notice this and ask yourself what "an interesting life" would mean in your own words. The best one can do with one's life, for Rorty, is to find one's own words for it.
fomo.practice: Finish the sentence in writing: "An interesting life for me is…" — without using a single word from the feed.

sleepless.text: At three in the morning thoughts are especially fond of "final" language — "always", "never", "it's all lost" — and final words were exactly what Rorty trusted least. Sleeplessness and darkness make every thought enormous. Rorty taught us to notice which words we use to describe our lives. The ironist knows that no description — even one that is very convincing in the dark — is the last truth. The night vocabulary is only one of many, and in the morning it usually sounds different. You needn't argue with every thought or settle everything before dawn. It is enough to note: "this is a night description" — and let it wait until morning, when there will be other voices and other words around.
sleepless.practice: Silently stick the label "night description" on each intrusive thought and bring your attention back to your breath. Nothing more is needed — you can argue with it in the morning.

betrayal.text: Many moral dilemmas, Rorty wrote, are not a struggle of good against evil but a clash of different loyalties. Betrayal wounds deeply: what collapses is not only trust in a person but the very "we" you lived in. Understanding the other person's motives need not justify anything: the pain and humiliation of betrayal are real, and Rorty considered precisely these the things it is most important not to inflict. He described justice as "enlarged loyalty", and your capacity for loyalty hasn't gone anywhere just because it was betrayed. A destroyed "we" doesn't cancel your ability to trust. The fact that you knew how to be faithful remains yours, even if it wasn't valued.
betrayal.practice: Spend five minutes with someone you trust — in person or on the phone. You needn't talk about what happened: just feel that another "we" still exists.

jealousy.text: "Contingency" is one of Rorty's key words: no attachment is guaranteed by the nature of things, everything could have turned out otherwise. In jealousy this thought frightens: what if you're replaced, what if there's no room left for you in someone else's "we"? But it has another side: precisely because the bond isn't secured in advance, it is created and sustained — by attention, conversation, care. Jealousy shows how valuable this bond is to you, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. But you can look at it: what descriptions is it drawing — "I'm worse", "I'll be left"? These are possible stories, not proven facts. Sometimes it helps to test them in conversation rather than in imagination.
jealousy.practice: Write down one story your jealousy tells and underline only what is known for sure. The rest has been drawn in by fear.

resentment.text: The same story told in other words is, for Rorty, already a slightly different life: we create ourselves by redescribing our past. An old grudge is a heavy load, and it didn't come from nowhere: you really were hurt. But a grudge often clings to a single description of the past, repeated again and again in the same words. To redescribe doesn't mean denying the harm or necessarily forgiving. It means finding other words for that story, in which you are not only the one who was hurt but also the one who goes on living. The past is not frozen: its meaning changes depending on how we tell it. The grudge can remain part of the story but stop being the whole story.
resentment.practice: Take a five-minute walk and tell yourself this old story as you go — but end it not with the one who hurt you but with the words "And then I…".

heartbreak.text: A song, a street, the smell of coffee: following Freud, Rorty believed that any small thing can carry enormous weight in someone's life. A person is a web of the finest, contingent connections, in which words, places and habits are woven into what we call ourselves. The one you loved was woven into many threads of your web, which is why the parting echoes everywhere: in routes, jokes, plans. The pain of a broken heart is evidence of how deeply you loved, and it deserves time. The web doesn't tear forever; it gets retied, slowly, thread by thread. Something of what you received in this relationship will stay in you — as new words and ways of seeing the world.
heartbreak.practice: Name the one thread that hurts most — a place, a song, a habit. Sit with it silently for a minute, a hand on your chest, without trying to get rid of it.

impostor.text: To know something, for Rorty, means being able to defend it in conversation with others, not carrying a flawless copy of reality in your head. Knowledge and competence for him are what a community finds convincing in the course of practice and conversation, not a hidden essence you might "actually" lack. The fear of being "found out" at any moment visits very capable people. It rests on an imaginary figure of the "real expert", next to whom you are supposedly a fake. But there is no such standard: there are people who learn, make mistakes and get things done together. You are not a copy of a standard but a participant in this conversation, and your participation is already part of what makes the work work.
impostor.practice: Ask a colleague or friend: "What do you think I'm good at?" Hear the answer without arguing — it is the voice of the community, not flattery.

self_hatred.text: If a person had one final description, the inner critic would be right. But Rorty believed no such description exists: any description is just one of many, not the truth about your essence. Self-hatred speaks as if it were passing the last verdict, and you don't have to agree with it. Rorty also said that cruelty is the worst thing we do, and that humiliation wounds especially — when everything you hold dear is made to look worthless. The inner critic does exactly that: it is cruel to you. And such cruelty can be treated the way you'd treat cruelty to others: by not granting that it's right. You deserve the same care that you might readily give to someone else.
self_hatred.practice: Imagine someone saying your inner critic's sentence to your friend. What would you answer? Say that answer to yourself — out loud or in a whisper.

helplessness.text: In "Achieving Our Country" Rorty defended the reformist left: the world is changed not by one great leap but by thousands of small improvements made by many people. Feeling powerless to change anything is a heavy experience, and Rorty was a realist: he didn't believe the world could be remade by a single great theory. Powerlessness partly comes from the feeling that everything should depend on you alone. But change, for Rorty, is always collective: many "we"s make it. This doesn't cancel the fact that right now there is much you can't change. But it lifts from you the impossible task of changing everything. The hope he wrote about starts small — with one thing you can reach today.
helplessness.practice: Look around and find one thing, however small, within your reach in the next hour. You needn't do it — just notice that it is there.

procrastination.text: For Dewey, Rorty's teacher in spirit, all thinking is an experiment: we try, see what happened, and correct. When you can't get started, it's easy to blame yourself for laziness, but things are usually more complicated. Often we wait for the "right" beginning: a perfect plan, complete certainty, a final formulation. Rorty, though, believed there are no final formulations at all — only working versions that improve along the way. An experiment that never started can teach nothing. Your first step doesn't have to be correct; it just has to exist, so that there is something to improve. A rough draft is not a failure but the ordinary form of any beginning. So a bad start is already much more than none at all.
procrastination.practice: Set a timer for two minutes and make the clumsiest rough draft of the first step. Allow it to be bad — this is an experiment, not an exam.

uprooted.text: Rorty called an ironist someone who has once realised that their native "final vocabulary" is only one of many. Emigration often makes a person an ironist against their will: words that seemed natural at home don't work here. Being cut off from home is a deep experience: not only daily life collapses but also the language in which you were used to understanding the world. It hurts, and Rorty didn't say it was easy. But he stressed that a "we" is not given forever: it can be widened and created anew. You live between vocabularies — and this is not only a loss but also a wealth: you know what can be seen only from two shores. Roots can become not a single point but a web of connections.
uprooted.practice: Say out loud a word from your native language or place that is hard to translate, and explain it — to yourself or to someone nearby. What does it mean to you?

overload.text: The conversation of mankind that Rorty loved so much will carry on perfectly well even if you don't hear every line of it. Overload and the endless feed wear you out: it seems you must know everything and have an opinion on everything. Rorty valued many voices and vocabularies, but he didn't think everyone is obliged to contain them all. He distinguished private life — your own passions and ways of creating yourself — from public life, where we try to reduce others' suffering. Not every bit of information noise requires your participation. You can choose which voices truly enrich your vocabulary and which merely take up space. Such selectiveness is not escape but care for your attention.
overload.practice: Put your phone away for five minutes and let no new voice into your conversation. Then decide which one source can be set aside until tomorrow.

unreality.text: In "Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature" Rorty argued against the picture in which the mind is an inner mirror separated from the world by a veil of representations. It is precisely within such a picture that the question arises: is what I see real? The feeling that everything is somehow not real can be very frightening, and it deserves respectful attention. Rorty, following Davidson, believed that we have never lost contact with the world: we are in it — through the body, actions, conversations with others. Even when the sense of reality is muted, you go on being in the world and among people. Simple actions and shared words help you return to this.
unreality.practice: Pick up an object and describe it out loud: its weight, temperature, texture. Then do one simple action — pour some water, open a window.

awe.text: Can someone who believes in nothing "superhuman" feel reverence? Rorty answered with his very life: he dreamed of a culture where nothing is worshipped as a divinity, and yet all his life he was full of admiration — for poems, orchids, brave deeds. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious feeling, and it needs no metaphysical explanation to be real. You can simply stand before a mountain, the sea, music or a human act and feel that it is greater than you. Such a moment is worth not analysing but living through and perhaps finding words for — for new words, according to Rorty, are exactly how we enrich life.
awe.practice: Describe what filled you with awe in one sentence to someone close — by voice or by message. Don't look for the right words; look for your own.

relief.text: Some philosophical problems, Rorty believed after Wittgenstein and Dewey, are not solved but dissolved: one day you notice that the question no longer holds you, because the very description of the situation has changed. Relief sometimes comes just like this — like an out-breath after long tension: not thanks to a final answer, but because the heaviness has stopped being the main thing. This too is a real resolution, and you can simply live it. There's no need to look straight away for what to do next. You can let yourself notice how your breathing, shoulders and gaze have changed — and thank yourself and others for having come through it. Rorty never thought every change has to be explained straight away.
relief.practice: Take a slow out-breath and notice where in your body you feel the relief. Stay with it for a few breaths, planning nothing.

calm.text: Rorty once spoke approvingly of philosophical "lightness" and even "superficiality": the ability to live and act without demanding final answers to the big questions. Calm is a precious state, and it needs no justification. It is not indifference but freedom from the need to ground everything completely. The ironist knows their vocabulary is not the last one, and so can live without the constant strain of proof. Rorty didn't think life must constantly be checked against eternal foundations; sometimes it is enough that things are good right now. The world doesn't have to come together into one system right now. You can simply stay in this quiet moment — it is real, even if it settles nothing forever.
calm.practice: Spend a minute in silence and find three things around you that ask no answer of you right now.

inspiration.text: Galileo, Hegel, Yeats — for Rorty these are people who invented a new language that sounded strange at first and then changed how everyone sees the world. Inspiration is the moment when such new words and images come to you. Rorty wrote about the "strong poet" — a person who creates themselves by finding their own language instead of an inherited one. Your inspiration is taking part in the most important thing language can do: renewal. There's no need to bring your ideas to perfection straight away. New metaphors are always clumsy at first and seem strange even to their author. What matters is to catch them while they're alive; you can polish them later. Rorty even believed that this is exactly how the history of culture moves — through lucky, contingent metaphors.
inspiration.practice: Write down the idea right now, as it is, even clumsily. Don't edit — keep the living version.

schadenfreude.text: For Rorty, the line between "us" and "them" runs where we stop noticing the details of someone else's pain. Schadenfreude is an awkward but very human feeling, and by itself it doesn't make you cruel. Following Judith Shklar, Rorty considered cruelty the worst thing we do, but he distinguished the private from the public: a fleeting feeling inside is one thing, an action that causes another pain is quite another. Schadenfreude often appears when we see a person as "one of them" rather than "one of us". And solidarity, for Rorty, grows from attention to the concrete details of others' pain. Schadenfreude can serve as a prompt: imagine the concrete life behind someone's failure. Usually the feeling then loses its force by itself.
schadenfreude.practice: Imagine one concrete evening of the person who failed: where they're sitting, what's on their table, whom they call. Notice what happens to your gloating.

contempt.text: "Idiot", "loser", "people like them" — Rorty noticed that we describe those we despise in one or two words beyond which our explanations don't go. He counted such words as part of a "final vocabulary". He saw clearly how people divide the world into "us" and "them" and how easy it is to deny "them" full humanity. Contempt often protects: it puts us higher so that it hurts less. The ironist, though, remembers that any vocabulary is only one possible description and can be revised. Contempt is a description that has stopped. You needn't force the feeling to change, but you can ask: what don't I know about this person's life? And what is my contempt protecting in me?
contempt.practice: Silently describe the person you despise in one sentence without evaluative words — only facts. Listen for what has changed.

disgust.text: In the lecture "Human Rights, Rationality, and Sentimentality" Rorty showed how easily people stop regarding others as fully human if those others repel them — and how stories widen the circle of sympathy. Disgust is a powerful feeling, and it often protects: the body says "no" to what is unacceptable to you. But many of our boundaries between the "normal" and the "disgusting" are not eternal truths but a legacy of history, culture and habit. Disgust at a situation can be an honest signal, but disgust at people or at yourself is worth checking — whose vocabulary is it speaking? Not everything that repels is evil, and not every revulsion tells the truth about you.
disgust.practice: Ask yourself under your breath: is this disgust about something that really does harm, or about something that is merely unfamiliar? Let the answer sound.

revenge.text: Who is the main character of your story? Rorty believed that a person creates themselves by redescribing what has happened to them — and in this sense revenge risks handing the lead role to the one who hurt you. The wish for revenge says: I was treated cruelly, and that matters. Rorty considered cruelty the worst thing people do to one another, so your grievance is legitimate. But something else follows too: revenge answers cruelty with cruelty and usually multiplies the pain in the world. There is a stronger path — to "redescribe" what happened so that the offender stops being the centre of the plot. Your story belongs to you. You can decide what place this wound will take in it, and not give it the leading role.
revenge.practice: Write one sentence about what happened in which you are the main character: "I went through…, and now I…"

anger_at_loved.text: Freud, as Rorty put it, helped us see that several selves live in each of us, each with its own story, and all of them a legitimate part of a person. Anger at those close to us is an ordinary part of any closeness, although we are often ashamed of it. Rorty wrote that Freud let us see any life as a poem woven from contingent events and memories. Anger at a loved one is not an exposure that "actually" you don't love them. It is the voice of one part of you, which has its own story and its own reasons. You don't have to choose between "I love" and "I'm angry". You can ask what the anger is saying, and put it into words without causing pain.
anger_at_loved.practice: Ask your anger, as you would a friend: "What do you need?" Listen to the answer and think how to tell it to your loved one without reproach.

ambivalence.text: Rorty never managed to fit Trotsky and the wild orchids into one picture — the fight against others' suffering and his own odd private passion — and in the end decided he didn't have to. He told of this in the essay of the same name: a life may have no single common denominator. Loving and being unable to stand the same person at once is agonising, especially if one of the feelings seems "false". But contradictory feelings towards someone close needn't be reduced to one "true" formula. Both sides can be the truth of your life. The ironist doesn't demand a wholeness from himself that isn't there. This doesn't make the relationship fake — it makes it human.
ambivalence.practice: Draw two columns on a sheet: "what I love" and "what I find hard". Don't try to reconcile them — just let them stand side by side.

guilty_relief.text: "A good daughter", "a devoted husband" — Rorty would see in such words part of a "final vocabulary" handed down to us by other people and circumstances, along with ready-made rules about what one may and may not feel. Relief after an ending — a break-up, the end of a loved one's long illness — often arrives together with shame. It doesn't cancel love. Relief seems shameful only as long as you describe yourself in other people's words. The same situation can be described differently: a long strain has ended, and you can finally breathe. Relief and love don't argue with each other — they are parts of one human story. Rorty insisted that an inherited vocabulary can be revised — including the vocabulary of what one is "supposed" to feel.
guilty_relief.practice: Imagine a beloved friend in your place. Say out loud to them one sentence about their relief — and listen to it yourself.

indifference.text: In his chapter on Nabokov, Rorty examines a special kind of cruelty — incuriosity: Humbert in "Lolita" and Kinbote in "Pale Fire" wound not out of malice but because they simply fail to notice someone else's pain. When you're untouched by what "should" touch you, it's easy to be frightened: am I like that? But Rorty has a gentle side too. He believed that sympathy is not an innate organ that you either have or lack, but something that grows through stories, details, attention. Indifference is not a verdict on your soul. Perhaps you're tired, or there wasn't enough concreteness. The feeling may come when one living detail appears. Or it may not — and that is human too.
indifference.practice: Choose one detail of what leaves you untouched — a name, a face, a circumstance. Rest your gaze on it for a minute without demanding that you feel anything.

escape.text: For Rorty, life is like a text that can be rewritten: self-creation is the ability to tell a new story about yourself and find words for who you want to be. The urge to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — is not a whim but a signal: the old description of your life no longer fits. Perhaps you've outgrown your former "vocabulary". But a life can be redescribed in different ways: sometimes you need to leave, and sometimes it's enough to name and arrange what you already have in a new way. What matters is to understand which description you want to leave and which one you want to find — and not to make big decisions in the hardest minute.
escape.practice: Write your life in one sentence as it sounds now, and below it — as you would like it to sound. Which word changed?

forbidden_attraction.text: Rorty drew a line through every human life: on one side the private, where we seek our own language, desires and ways of self-creation; on the other the public, where the main thing is not to cause others pain. Being drawn to someone unavailable or "not the one" is disorienting: the feeling is there, but there's no place for it in your life. The attraction itself belongs to your private story and is not yet an act; there's no reason to shame yourself for it. But it can be interesting: what does this desire say about what you lack, about who you want to become? You can study it the way you'd read a novel about yourself — attentively and without rushing to conclusions.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Ask yourself: what word describes what draws me — not the person, but a quality? Think where else in your life this quality could appear.

social_anxiety.text: "We", for Rorty, is not given but made: the circle of "our own" widens when you suddenly notice a familiar small thing in a stranger. Solidarity arises not from a shared essence but from the ability to see another as "one of us". When the fear of being judged is strong, it seems everyone is watching and judging — as if you see all the others as "one of them", evaluating and alien. But they too are probably afraid of something, embarrassed, worried about the impression they make. Rorty believed that attention to the concrete details of other lives widens the circle of "us". The fear of judgement can grow quieter if you remember: around you are people just as vulnerable as you.
social_anxiety.practice: Next time you're among people, look for a sign of nerves in someone — a gesture, a pause, an embarrassed smile. Tell yourself: "There's another one of us."

uncertainty.text: For twenty-five centuries philosophy searched for a firm foundation — an eternal truth to lean on — and Rorty suggested we stop digging. There are no such foundations, he believed: our language and our beliefs are contingent, formed historically, and could have been different. It sounds alarming, but Rorty saw freedom in it and proposed replacing the search for certainty with hope — hope that the future can become better if we work on it. Uncertainty wears you out: you want to know what will happen, and there's no knowing. But this is not a malfunction; it is the ordinary condition of human life. Without knowing the future, you can still choose what to hope for and what to do today.
uncertainty.practice: Walk for a few minutes, and at every turn swap the question "what will happen?" for "what do I hope for, and what can I do today?".

waiting.text: Thought, for Dewey and Rorty, exists not for contemplation but for acting and coping with life. That is why waiting — for an answer, results, news — is so hard: it seems you can't act, everything is being decided somewhere else. But you can ask: what useful thing can I do now, while there's no answer? Sometimes it's preparing for different outcomes, sometimes it's turning to something else entirely. Rorty loved the image of an ongoing "conversation of mankind" whose outcome is not known in advance. Waiting is also part of the conversation, not an empty pause in life. In it you can talk about other things. Rorty was always more interested in the next step than in a final answer.
waiting.practice: Write two short plans: "if the answer is yes…" and "if it's no…". Then put the sheet aside and do something else.

regret.text: Shortly before his death, already gravely ill, Rorty wrote a short essay, "The Fire of Life", and admitted in it that he wished he had given more time to poetry. He said it calmly, without self-flagellation, as an honest observation. Regret over what you did or didn't do can hold on for a long time. But the past can be "redescribed": not undone, but told anew, seeing in it not only mistakes but also what you could and couldn't do back then. The ironist knows that their former self spoke a different vocabulary. Then regret becomes not a verdict but material for a new story about yourself — and a hint at what matters to you now.
regret.practice: Read aloud one poem or a few lines you love. Then silently finish the sentence: "What I regret tells me that what matters to me is…"

quote.text: I now wish that I had spent somewhat more of my life with verse.
quote.author: Richard Rorty

longing.text: What makes people real to us is not general qualities but details: how a person laughs, what they say in the mornings, their pet words. This is one of Rorty's warmest thoughts: moral life grows not from abstractions but from love for particular people. That is why missing a particular person hurts so much: it is precisely them you lack, with all their peculiarities. Your longing is the other side of this concreteness. You miss not "a good person in general" but exactly this one. And that is a sign of how real they were, or still are, to you. Such longing is a form of memory and faithfulness.
longing.practice: Write down three details about this person that perhaps only you know.

world_pain.text: "Sentimental education" was Rorty's name for the path along which other people's pain — through stories and the details of their lives — begins to touch you too. He considered this the chief moral achievement. Hurting for the world — over hard news, wars, injustice — can be very heavy, and it is a sign that your circle of sympathy is wide. But Rorty was also a pragmatist: he suggested not drowning in general horror but looking for the concrete — concrete people, concrete deeds. Hope, for him, is not certainty of a good outcome but readiness to work for it. You are not obliged to carry all the world's pain. Your response is the beginning of solidarity, not a cause for despair.
world_pain.practice: Choose one concrete, manageable action for someone who is having a hard time right now — even a very small one — and do it today.

quote.text: …hope that suffering will be diminished, that the humiliation of human beings by other human beings may cease.
quote.author: Richard Rorty

rejection.text: "The world does not speak. Only we do," Rorty wrote: the world has no language of its own and passes no verdicts on our worth. Rejection wounds precisely because it seems a final verdict. But every judgement is a description made by a particular person in a particular situation, in their words. When you were rejected, that was one description, not the truth about you. The other person was looking through their own "final vocabulary", in which there was no place for you. That hurts. But it doesn't mean there is no place for you anywhere. Your worth is not determined by one other person's description, and other descriptions exist too.
rejection.practice: Get in touch with someone who values you and talk about something ordinary. Let their voice remind you that other descriptions of you exist.

quote.text: The world does not speak. Only we do.
quote.author: Richard Rorty

abandonment.text: Closeness, for Rorty, is not found once and for all — it is made again and again: by attention, care, shared stories, the way a conversation is made. On the one hand, this is unsettling: there are no guarantees. On the other, it gives hope: a bond can be built and strengthened; it is not predetermined by fate. The fear of being abandoned can be very strong, especially if you have been left before. But it tells the future as if it were already decided and written down. The future, for Rorty, is open: many hands write it, and yours is among them. You can invest in the bonds you have now and notice how they hold.
abandonment.practice: Recall one bond that has survived a hard time, and do something small for it today — call, send greetings, ask how they are.

unrequited.text: No one can make another person speak their language — Rorty, for whom life was made of vocabularies and stories, understood this soberly. Unrequited love is a pain full of silence: the feeling is huge, and there's no answer. Rorty considered love for a particular person one of the deepest experiences, from which all moral life grows. Your love is real and valuable in itself, even if it went unanswered. It showed what you are capable of: seeing another in detail, caring, hoping. The lack of an answer is not a verdict on you; your stories simply didn't coincide. It hurts, but it doesn't cancel your capacity to love.
unrequited.practice: Put a hand on your heart and tell yourself one thing you have learned about yourself thanks to this love.

humiliation.text: In "1984" O'Brien is after more than pain: he wants Winston himself to betray what he loved. Rorty analysed this scene in detail and saw in it the essence of humiliation — making what mattered to a person look worthless. Humiliation is one of the deepest wounds, a special form of cruelty. That is why, for Rorty, it is so important to remember: no language of description — neither yours nor anyone else's — is the final truth about a person. Whoever humiliated you imposed their description on you. But you have a right to your own. The words in which you speak about yourself and your values can be reclaimed gradually.
humiliation.practice: Name out loud, in one or two words, what mattered to you before this humiliation and still matters. Calmly repeat them once more.

body_shame.text: Once upon a time quite different bodies were considered "beautiful" than today — Rorty would say that the vocabulary changed, not the truth. He showed that much of what seems a natural norm is a "final vocabulary" that took shape historically. Words like "beautiful", "right", "excess" acquire meaning within a particular culture and era. Dissatisfaction with your body can be very persistent: the mirror, photos, other people's glances. But your body is being judged in words that are not eternal truth. You can notice where these words come from and try to describe your body differently: not as an object of evaluation but as what allows you to live, hug, move, feel. Of any words, Rorty suggested asking not "are they true?" but "do they help us live?"
body_shame.practice: Make one movement that feels good — stretch, roll your shoulders — and silently name three things your body does, rather than how it looks.

illness.text: Rorty did not demand a higher meaning from life, and this frees us from one heavy question: illness doesn't have to be a lesson or a trial. It changes a great deal: the body you relied on lets you down, and familiar life shifts. Fear, anger, tiredness are legitimate here. Pain, Rorty wrote, is something "pre-linguistic", something that links us with all living beings. So suffering is a shared experience, not a personal failure, and no one is to blame for their body being ill. Illness doesn't need to be justified by a beautiful description. But you are still the author of your story: you choose the words in which to tell of a life that includes illness. And illness is not the whole of your life.
illness.practice: Tell someone close to you one thing that was hard today and one thing that was good.

pride.text: Rorty's word for how a person creates themselves was self-creation: finding one's own words and one's own deeds rather than repeating others'. You have made something, endured something, seen something through — and being proud of it is a good, healthy feeling. It is the moment when you recognise yourself in what you've done: not because it's better than others' work but because it is yours. Rorty didn't believe in eternal foundations or higher authorities: no one from above needs to confirm the value of what you did. It is enough that it matters to you and perhaps to the people around you. Let yourself be glad of it, without downplaying or apologising.
pride.practice: Tell someone about what you're proud of, in plain words and without disclaimers like "oh, it's nothing".

melancholy.text: For Rorty, Proust was the model ironist: again and again he redescribed departed people and places until his life became a novel. He wasn't looking for an eternal truth about himself — he peered into the past and recast it in words. Rorty also valued that Proust didn't try to rise above his past but simply let it sound. Gentle melancholy, in which sadness sits beside tenderness, resembles such work. It is a moment when you look tenderly at what has been and gone, and it becomes part of your story. In this light melancholy needn't be treated as an illness or fixed — it has its own beauty.
melancholy.practice: Write down, in a few words, one memory that resonates now — as the first sentence of a small novel.
